entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen19945" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19946" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19947" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19947" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19946" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19948" type="x-p"/> The blessedness of the man who is merciful to the poor, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.1-Psa.41.3">Psa 41:1-3</reference>. The psalmist complains of his enemies, and prays for support, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.4-Psa.41.10">Psa 41:4-10</reference>; and blesses God for having heard his prayer, and preserved him from his adversaries, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.11">Psa 41:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.12">Psa 41:12</reference>. A fine doxology closes the Psalm, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.13">Psa 41:13</reference>. <div eID="gen19948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19949" type="x-p"/> The title as before. The Syriac says it was "A Psalm of David, when he appointed overseers to take care of the poor." The Arabic says, "It is a prophecy concerning the incarnation; and also of the salutation of Judas." It appears to me to have been written on the same occasion as the three former, and to relate to David's malady and cure, and the evil treatment he had from his enemies during his affliction. Our Lord, by accommodation, applies the ninth verse to the treachery of Judas, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.18">Joh 13:18</reference>; but as to any other direct reference to Christ, or his history, I believe the Psalm has none. <div eID="gen19949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19950" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19951" type="x-p"/> Blessed is he that considereth - God is merciful; he will have man to resemble him: as far as he is merciful, feels a compassionate heart, and uses a benevolent hand, he resembles his Maker; and the mercy he shows to others God will show to him. But it is not a sudden impression at the sight of a person in distress, which obliges a man to give something for the relief of the sufferer, that constitutes the merciful character. It is he who considers the poor; who endeavors to find them out; who looks into their circumstances; who is in the habit of doing so; and actually, according to his power and means, goes about to do good; that is the merciful man, of whom God speaks with such high approbation, and to whom he promises a rich reward.

The psalmist complains of his enemies, and prays for support, Psa 41:4-10 ; and blesses God for having heard his prayer, and preserved him from his adversaries, Psa 41:11 , Psa 41:12 . The Arabic says, "It is a prophecy concerning the incarnation; and also of the salutation of Judas." It appears to me to have been written on the same occasion as the three former, and to relate to David's malady and cure, and the evil treatment he had from his enemies during his affliction. Our Lord, by accommodation, applies the ninth verse to the treachery of Judas, Joh 13:18 ; but as to any other direct reference to Christ, or his history, I believe the Psalm has none. entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19952" type="x-p"/> The Lord will preserve him, and keep him alive - It is worthy of remark, that benevolent persons, who consider the poor, and especially the sick poor; who search cellars, garrets, back lanes, and such abodes of misery, to find them out, (even in the places where contagion keeps its seat), very seldom fall a prey to their own benevolence. The Lord, in an especial manner, keeps them alive, and preserves them; while many, who endeavor to keep far from the contagion, are assailed by it, and fall victims to it. God loves the merciful man.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19953" type="x-p"/> The Lord will strengthen him - Good, benevolent, and merciful as he is, he must also die: but he shall not die as other men; he shall have peculiar consolations, refreshment, and support, while passing through the valley of the shadow of death. <div eID="gen19953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19954" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt make all his bed - הפכת haphachta, thou hast turned up, tossed, and shaken it; and thou wilt do so to all his bed - thou wilt not leave one uneasy place in it - not one lump, or any unevenness, to prevent him from sleeping. Thou wilt do every thing, consistently with the accomplishment of the great decree, "Unto dust thou shalt return," to give him ease, refreshment, and rest. We may sum up the privileges of the merciful man: <div eID="gen19954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19955" type="x-p"/> 1. He is generally blessed, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.1">Psa 41:1</reference>. <div eID="gen19955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19956" type="x-p"/> 2. He will be delivered in the time of trouble, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.1">Psa 41:1</reference>. <div eID="gen19956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19957" type="x-p"/> 3. He will be preserved by a particular providence, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.2">Psa 41:2</reference>. <div eID="gen19957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19958" type="x-p"/> 4. He shall be kept alive amidst infection and danger, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.2">Psa 41:2</reference>. <div eID="gen19958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19959" type="x-p"/> 5. He shall be blessed on the earth in his temporal concerns, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.2">Psa 41:2</reference>. <div eID="gen19959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19960" type="x-p"/> 6. His enemies shall not be able to spoil or destroy him, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.2">Psa 41:2</reference>. <div eID="gen19960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19961" type="x-p"/> 7. He shall be strengthened on a bed of languishing, to enable him to bear his afflictions, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.3">Psa 41:3</reference>. <div eID="gen19961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19962" type="x-p"/> 8. He shall have ease, comfort, and support in his last hours, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.3">Psa 41:3</reference>.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19968" type="x-p"/> An evil disease, say they, cleaveth fast unto him - דבר בליעל יצוק בו debar beliyaal yatsuk bo, a thing, word, or pestilence of Belial, is poured out upon him. entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19970" type="x-p"/> Mine own familiar friend - This is either a direct prophecy of the treachery of Judas, or it is a fact in David's distresses which our Lord found so similar to the falsity of his treacherous disciple, that he applies it to him, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.18">Joh 13:18</reference>. What we translate mine own familiar friend, איש שלומי ish shelomi, is the man of my peace. The man who, with the שלום לך shalom lecha, peace be to thee! kissed me; and thus gave the agreed-on signal to my murderers that I was the person whom they should seize, hold fast, and carry away. <div eID="gen19970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19971" type="x-p"/> Did eat of my bread - Was an inmate in my house. Applied by our Lord to Judas, when eating with him out of the same dish. See <reference osisRef="Joh.13.18">Joh 13:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.26">Joh 13:26</reference>. Possibly it may refer to Ahithophel, his counsellor, the man of his peace, his prime minister; who, we know, was the strength of Absalom's conspiracy.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19973" type="x-p"/> By this I know that thou favorest me - If thou hadst not been on my side, I had perished by this disease; and then my enemies would have had cause to triumph. <div eID="gen19973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19974" type="x-p"/> This also has been applied to our Lord; and Calmet says it is the greatest proof we have of the divinity of Christ, that he did not permit the malice of the Jews, nor the rage of the devil, to prevail against him. They might persecute, blaspheme, mock, insult, crucify, and slay him; but his resurrection confounded them; and by it he gained the victory over sin, death, and hell.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen19977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19978" type="x-p"/> Blessed be the Lord God of Israel - By all these circumstances and events glory shall redound to the name of God for ever; for the record of these things shall never perish, but be published from one generation to another; and it has been so. <div eID="gen19978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19979" type="x-p"/> From everlasting, and to everlasting - מהעולם ועד העולם mehaolam vead haolam; From the hidden time to the hidden time; from that which had no beginning to that which has no end. <div eID="gen19979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19980" type="x-p"/> To which he subscribes, Amen and Amen. Fiat, fiat - Vulgate. Γενοιτο, γενοιτο - Septuagint. The Chaldee says, "And let the righteous say, Amen, and Amen." "Be blessed, Lord God of Israel, from world, and in world. Be it! So be it!" - Anglo-Saxon. To which the Old Psalter approaches very nearly: Blyssed Lord God of Isrel, fra werld, and in werld: Be it done! be it done. Thus illustrated by the same, Fra werld in werld; that es, fra the bygynnyng of this wereld, in til wereld that lastes ay. Be it done, be it done. This dubblying schews that it es at do of al men. In Latyn, it es, fiat, fiat! in Ebru, Amen Amen es writyn: tharfore that Aquila translated vere, vel fideliter, that es, sothfastly or trew. <div eID="gen19980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19981" type="x-p"/> Thus ends what the Hebrews call the first book of Psalms; for the reader will recollect that this book is divided by the Jews into five books, the first of which ends with this Psalm. <div eID="gen19981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19982" type="x-p"/> This doxology, Dr. Kennicott supposes, may have been added by the collector of this book; and he thinks that the division into books is not arbitrary, and that the Psalms were collected at different times by different persons. See the Introduction. There is certainly a considerable variety in the style of the several books; in the examination of which the Hebrew critic will not lose his labor.  <chapter eID="Ps.41"/> <div eID="gen19982" type="x-p"/>
